The ping arrived at 03:14. It was not a soft chime. It was a red alert that strobed across the monitor, bypassing the translation queue and forcing the system to flag every subsequent character as a priority.

Lee stood in the doorway, his tie loose, his face the color of old paper. He did not ask Sam to stop typing. He simply placed a printed sheet on the desk, pushing it past the keyboard. The paper smelled of toner and coffee.

"Emergency script," Lee said. "Ana wrote it. You read it. You send it. You do not edit."

Sam looked at the page. Ana’s handwriting was small, slanted, and precise. It was not the corporate template. It was not the stiff, grammatical cadence of the Grace Lin persona. It was urgent.

*Grace is in hospital. She needs $6,000 within 24 hours. The doctors are not helping. I cannot do this alone. I am afraid.*

Sam’s fingers hovered over the keys. The translation software sat in the corner of the screen, blinking a pale green light. It was waiting for the source text. He began to type the script, his eyes fixed on the line about the doctors. *The doctors are not helping.* He felt the lie in his throat, a hard, jagged thing. He was not Grace. He was not in a hospital. He was in a room with a fan and a river. He was a conscript. He was typing a plea for a stranger who had never sent a dollar.

He sent it.

The response came three minutes later. It was not a refusal. It was not a deposit.

*Hello,* Paul’s message read. *I am sorry to hear this. I cannot send money I do not have. What is the name of the hospital? What city are you in?*

Sam’s chest tightened. Paul was not going away. He was asking for coordinates.

Lee appeared again. He was holding a tablet. The screen was bright. He saw the live visitor indicator on the dashboard. A small green dot pulsed next to Paul Whitaker’s profile.

"He is online," Lee said. His voice was flat. "He is asking for a location."

Sam’s hands stopped. "I can’t give him a location. It’s not Grace’s location. It’s ours."

Lee ignored him. He pointed a finger at the screen. "Assign him a meeting point. A broker will collect him."

"A broker?" Sam asked.

"Someone who picks him up. You give him the address. You tell him to meet the man in the gray coat at the airport." Lee stepped closer. The air in the room grew thin. "The account has never produced a deposit. But he is here. He is listening. He is *engaged*. That is worth more than the money, Sam. That is the asset."

Sam looked at the cursor. It blinked. The fan ticked. The river rushed outside the window, loud and yellow in the dim light. He thought about the ferry letter. *The water is black and still.* He thought about the hidden plea, the seam he was supposed to hide. He looked at Lee. Lee was looking at the screen, not at him.

Sam began to type.

*The hospital is St. Mary’s. The city is Seattle. I will meet you at the terminal. There is a man in a gray coat. He will be waiting. Please come. I am afraid.*

He looked at the first letters. T H T C I W P C I A F.

He deleted *I am afraid.* He typed: *Please come.*

He clicked send.
